Omarchy channel guide

omarchy-dev on Omarchy

Omarchy built from the tip of the quattro dev branch — tomorrow's desktop today, for testers who snapshot first.

Reviewed 2026-11-05 · independent editorial guide

Short answer

Install with omarchy pkg add omarchy-dev (about 2 minutes; 67.6 MB download / 72 MB installed) — but read the warning first: this replaces your core Omarchy system package with a bleeding-edge build. Don't install it on a daily driver; use a VM or spare machine, snapshot first with omarchy snapshot create, and update only through omarchy update. Roll back from the Limine boot menu.

omarchy-dev on Omarchy

omarchy-dev is Omarchy itself — the same DHH-built Arch + Hyprland desktop — packaged from the tip of the in-development quattro branch instead of a tagged stable release, for people who want to test tomorrow’s Omarchy today.

TL;DR

omarchy pkg add omarchy-dev

Takes ~2 minutes to download (67.6 MB download / 72 MB installed, per the store listing).

Stop and read this first: this is not an app you add alongside Omarchy. It replaces your core Omarchy system package with a bleeding-edge build. If your machine is your daily driver and it works today, do not install this on it — install it in a VM, or on a spare machine you can afford to break. The official manual reserves the dev channel for “an experienced Linux user, working directly on Omarchy, and willing to tolerate breakage.”

Getting started (5 minutes)

1. The mental model.

Omarchy ships in four update channels: stable (tagged releases, on an Arch mirror running about a month behind upstream), RC (final validation before a major release), edge (latest dev builds + latest Arch packages), and dev (Omarchy linked directly to a git checkout of the source in ~/omarchy, combined with edge packages). omarchy-dev is the packaged form of that dev tip: the same curated Hyprland desktop, terminal, editor, and agent tooling as the main omarchy package, just with the newest, potentially unstable changes applied first. It exists so testers and contributors can track development in real time instead of waiting for tagged releases — v4.5.0-rc1 landed Oct 20, 2026, rc2 Oct 27, rc3 Nov 2, roughly one a week, and the dev build is ahead of all of them.

2. Decide where to install it.

The store listing’s own “Good to know” says: a machine (or VM) that can run Arch Linux, plus tolerance for in-development, potentially unstable changes. The safe order of preference:

  1. A VM — the best place to try it. Breakage costs you a snapshot restore, not your workday.
  2. A spare machine — fine if you can reinstall it without pain.
  3. Your daily driver — only if you are comfortable recovering a broken Arch system from a snapshot, and you have a current backup of /home.

3. Snapshot first, then install.

omarchy snapshot create   # manual rollback point — do this BEFORE installing
omarchy pkg add omarchy-dev
omarchy version           # confirm what you're now running

Why the manual snapshot: the update flow takes its own snapshot, but a channel/package switch can leave you without a snapshot of the old system — a documented trap in a real 4.0.6 → 4.5 RC upgrade walkthrough, where the automatic snapshot was taken only after the new packages were already installed. Take your own first; it costs seconds.

4. Update the dev way.

Once you’re on the dev build, updates work the same as stable — through Omarchy’s own flow, not raw pacman:

omarchy update            # snapshot, packages, migrations — the only supported path

omarchy update takes a Btrfs snapshot first (it needs at least 10 GiB free), updates the Omarchy packages, runs any pending migrations, and updates system packages from the Omarchy Arch mirror plus AUR. A direct sudo pacman -Syu is blocked by a pacman hook (“Woah partner…”) that points you back to omarchy update — that guard exists so you never skip the snapshot and migrations.

5. The three things everyone needs to know:

  • This is the whole OS, not an app. There is no “launch omarchy-dev” step. After install and a reboot you are simply running a newer, unreleased Omarchy. Your desktop, hotkeys, and tools look the same — until a dev change alters them, which is the point.
  • Your customizations live in ~/.config, not in the shipped tree. Since Quattro (Omarchy 4), Omarchy’s internals are system-managed packages rather than a mutable git checkout in your home directory, specifically so your modifications stay separate from shipped files. Treat the installed Omarchy system tree as read-only; anything you change inside it can be overwritten by an update. (The dev channel is the exception in spirit — it links to a git checkout in ~/omarchy — so if you edit files there, expect updates to stash or overwrite your changes. Unverified: exact behavior on this build.)
  • Breakage is a when, not an if. The dev channel is where regressions are found. The recovery path is the snapshot: reboot, pick the pre-update snapshot in the Limine boot menu, and restore. Snapshots revert / (system packages and configs) but not /home, so a snapshot won’t recover deleted personal files or broken dotfiles in ~/.config — keep real backups.

Common issues & fixes

All items below come from the official manual, the repo, or published first-hand upgrade accounts — none are invented. There is no omarchy-dev-specific issue tracker (it’s the same repo as Omarchy itself, omacom/omarchy, 46,303 stars, ~7,600 commits), so the record for this exact package is thin; the issues below are the documented Omarchy update/channel failure modes that apply directly to running the dev tip.

Something broke after moving to the dev build — a hotkey, the bar, a theme, a tool

Fix: Roll back to your pre-install snapshot. Reboot, pick the snapshot in the Limine boot menu (snapshots are listed by date and Omarchy version), and confirm the restore — or run omarchy-snapshot restore / omarchy snapshot restore from the terminal. This is the documented recovery path in the manual: “If you ever have a problem after doing an update, you can rollback your system to the snapshot taken before the update.” If you skipped the manual snapshot in step 3, the update-time snapshot is your fallback — but only if one was taken before the dev packages landed. Unverified on Omarchy: the exact Limine menu labels on the dev build.

sudo pacman -Syu refuses to run — “Woah partner…” and a pointer back to omarchy update

Fix: Not a bug, it’s the guard. Omarchy blocks direct system upgrades so you don’t skip the snapshot, migrations, and config updates that omarchy update runs together with new packages. Use omarchy update (or its alias mup). The guard message tells you how to bypass it for a single transaction (OMARCHY_ALLOW_DIRECT_PACMAN=1) — but bypassing skips the snapshot and migrations, which is exactly what you don’t want on a dev build. Documented in the manual and confirmed by multiple independent guides.

I switched channels (or installed omarchy-dev) and now I have no snapshot of my old working system

Fix: This is the documented trap from a real 4.0.6 → 4.5.0 RC2 upgrade walkthrough: the channel-switch command runs its own omarchy update -y, and that update’s automatic snapshot is taken after the new packages are installed — so the switch alone leaves no snapshot of the old system. Prevention is the fix: always run omarchy snapshot create by hand before changing channels or installing omarchy-dev. If you’re already past it, your only rollback points are older snapshots (Snapper keeps the last five update-time snapshots) or a reinstall. Unverified: whether omarchy pkg add omarchy-dev itself triggers an update-style snapshot; assume it doesn’t until confirmed.

I want off the dev build and back to stable

Fix: Two routes, in order of gentleness. First try switching the channel back: omarchy channel set stable (or Update > Channel in the menu, Super + Space), then omarchy update. Unverified: whether that path cleanly downgrades dev packages that are newer than stable. The guaranteed route is the manual’s: omarchy reinstall — it reinstalls all default Omarchy packages, puts you on stable, and downgrades any packages that are too new. The cost is real: it resets all configuration files, and your user config changes to the Omarchy defaults will be overwritten. Back up ~/.config first.

My edits inside Omarchy’s own files vanished after an update

Fix: Expected behavior since Quattro: the shipped system tree is managed by packages, and updates overwrite it. Put every customization in your own config under ~/.config and leave the installed tree alone. On the dev build this bites harder, because dev updates land constantly and the git checkout in ~/omarchy is pulled fresh on update (the update tooling pulls with --autostash, so local changes get stashed, not merged). Unverified: exact autostash behavior on the packaged omarchy-dev install vs. a manual git checkout.

Pairs well with / If you hate this, try

Pairs well with

  • rumb (a read-only pre-update dashboard — run it before omarchy update on a dev box so you know what the next dev drop touches and whether it needs a reboot), linux-omarchy (Omarchy’s BORE-scheduler kernel — the dev build’s most-tested companion, and the kernel switcher omarchy-kernel lets you keep the stock Arch kernel alongside it as a fallback), and the Omarchy Discord #omarchy-release-candidates channel / GitHub issues (where dev regressions are actually reported and triaged — if you run dev, reporting what breaks is the job).

If you hate this, try

  • The stable omarchy package (omarchy pkg add omarchy) — the same desktop, on tagged releases with a month-behind Arch mirror; or the RC channel (omarchy channel set rc) if you want to help polish the next major release without living on the raw tip. Both are covered in the comparison below.

Comparison: omarchy-dev vs similar options

omarchy-devomarchy (stable)linux-omarchy
PriceFree (MIT)Free (MIT)Free (GPL-2.0-only)
What it isOmarchy built from the tip of the quattro dev branchOmarchy at the latest tagged releaseOmarchy’s custom kernel (BORE CPU + ADIOS I/O schedulers), v7.2.15-1
Best forTesters and contributors tracking Omarchy development in real timeEveryone — the daily driverA faster, more responsive kernel on an otherwise stable system
StabilityUnstable by design — regressions expected; manual: “willing to tolerate breakage”Stable; Arch mirror ~1 month behind upstream so incompatibilities get caught firstStable kernel, but a kernel change is still a system-level change
Omarchy installomarchy pkg add omarchy-devomarchy pkg add omarchy (or the ISO)omarchy pkg add linux-omarchy

Verdict: Run stable omarchy unless you have a specific reason to be on the tip — a bug you need to verify fixed, a feature you need early, or a contribution you’re testing. If you want to help without the full risk, the RC channel is the middle ground; if you want the dev feel with less risk, stable Omarchy plus the linux-omarchy kernel is a cheaper thrill. omarchy-dev is for the people who file the bug reports, not the people who read them.

omarchy-dev is the free alternative to waiting

omarchy-dev is the free alternative to waiting. What you give up: stability, and the month-behind Arch mirror that catches incompatibilities before they reach you. What you keep: everything else — the same desktop, the same tools, the same snapshot-and-rollback safety net. The price of “early” is paid in breakage, not money.

Frequently asked questions

What exactly is omarchy-dev?

The Omarchy Linux distribution, packaged from the tip of its in-development quattro branch rather than a stable release. Same curated Hyprland desktop, terminal, editor, and agent tooling as the main omarchy package — just with the newest, potentially unstable changes applied first. The repo’s default branch is quattro; as of Nov 5, 2026 it sits at ~7,600 commits with v4.5.0-rc3 (Nov 2, 2026) the latest tagged release.

Should I install omarchy-dev on my daily driver?

No — unless you are an experienced Linux user who can recover a broken system from a snapshot and you have current backups. The manual reserves the dev channel for people “working directly on Omarchy, and willing to tolerate breakage.” Everyone else should run stable omarchy, or try dev in a VM first.

Does installing omarchy-dev replace my stable Omarchy?

Yes. It swaps the core Omarchy system package for the dev-tip build — it is not a side-by-side app you launch. Your desktop will look the same until a dev change alters it. Unverified: the exact pacman replace/conflict behavior on install; confirm with pacman -Q omarchy omarchy-dev before and after.

How is omarchy-dev different from the edge channel?

They overlap but aren’t identical. Edge tracks the latest dev builds plus the latest Arch packages. Dev goes further: it links Omarchy directly to a git checkout of the source in ~/omarchy, combined with edge packages. omarchy-dev is the packaged form of that tip. Either way, both are tester territory — the manual says edge is only for people “experienced with Linux, and know how to recover a system that has problems.”

Something broke — how do I roll back?

Reboot and pick the pre-update snapshot in the Limine boot menu, then confirm the restore (or omarchy snapshot restore). Snapshots revert / but not /home. If the breakage is “I don’t want to be on dev anymore,” omarchy channel set stable + omarchy update is the gentle exit; omarchy reinstall is the guaranteed one, at the cost of resetting your Omarchy config files to defaults.
